units.translation: But if Pelias was sending them into danger, why did his son go along? And this one says, against his father's will; but Demagetus says that Pelias ordered the Argo to be built with loose bolts, so that it would quickly destroy them; but Argus did the opposite, and Acastus, trusting the builder, went aboard.

b. Argus, the goddess’s helper: because he built the Argo by Athena’s forethought. For this reason the poet says (I 19) that it came into being by Athena’s instructions.

b. Since the daughters of Minyas: for Minyas had many daughters. And indeed Jason is the son of Alcimede, daughter of Clymene, daughter of Minyas. Stesichorus (fg 54 B. III 225) says he is the son of Eteoclymene, and Pherecydes (3 fg 104 b J.) says he is the son of Alcimede, daughter of Phylacus. From Isonoe, daughter of Danaus and Zeus, was born Orchomenus, after whom the city Orchomenus is named; and from Orchomenus and Hermippe, daughter of Boeotus, was born Minyas — by surname, but in nature son of Poseidon — who lived in Orchomenus, from whom the

people were called Minyae; and from Minyas and Clytodora were born Presbon, Periclymene, and Eteoclymene, and from Phanosyra, daughter of Paeon, and Minyas were born Orchomenus, Diochthondes, and Athamas. But Demetrius of Scepsis (fg 51 Gaede) says that those who inhabit Iolcus are called Minyae.

238. Pagasae: a headland of Magnesia; it was named from the Argo having been built there. But the Scepsian (Demetrius of Scepsis fg 52 Gaede) says from the places being washed by springs. There is also a sanctuary of Apollo Pagasaeus.
240. Like stars among clouds: looking to their lineage, fortune, and courage, he calls the heroes stars, and the common crowds clouds.
